rows.why: Every MCP server and tool the AI can call is inventoried with an owner and an approval.
Retiring an MCP server or tool revokes its credentials and access without leaving the AI workflow broken or unmanaged.
The roles that approve, grant and own each MCP tool and its credentials are documented and known.
Policies set the security terms that outside MCP servers and their suppliers must meet before the AI uses them.
There is a contingency for when an outside tool or server fails or is compromised, and incident plans cover it.
The connections the AI has to internal systems, outside servers and external networks through its tools are documented.
Humans approve the tool actions the AI takes with its credentials, and that oversight is documented.
Outside MCP servers and suppliers the AI relies on are inventoried and their risks are mapped.
Metrics track the inputs and behaviour of third-party tools, and changes in their capabilities or authorization are watched.
Tool use in production is reviewed for anomalies and for calls outside the approved capabilities.
Tool access and authentication are tested adversarially, and the results of those tests are recorded.
Tool calls are logged with the identity and credentials used, so actions can be traced and accounted for.
Access to tools is limited by central authorization, least-privilege roles and throttling.
Procedures exist to contain and recover from an unauthorized tool call, including revoking tokens and disabling the tool.
Access to a tool or server can be revoked and the AI switched off from it when it behaves outside its approved use.
Outside MCP servers are classified by the data and systems they reach and their risks are monitored against organizational tolerance.
Tool-related incidents are reported, recorded with their impact and responses, and reviewed after the event.

review.reason: The row checks that roles for approving, granting and owning tools are documented, but its only safeguard MCP-6.1 is the access-granting process, not role definitions. Needs a roles safeguard such as MCP-17.5 or a roles and ownership control for tool access.

The row claims humans approve the tool actions the AI takes, but its only safeguard MCP-6.1 covers granting access, not human oversight of individual actions. MCP-17.4 (human confirmation enforcement) or a human-in-the-loop safeguard fits better.
